name: Ravangla
tagline: A 130 ft Buddha, old gompas and a ridge town between two hills
meta_description: Ravangla, South Sikkim: Buddha Park, Ralang Monastery, the Maenam Hill trek, Kewzing homestays, Pang Lhabsol, shared jeep fares and budget stays.
summary: Ravangla is a small ridge town at about 2,100 m in the Namchi district of South Sikkim, best known for the 130 ft Buddha at Tathagata Tsal. Use it as a cool, quiet base for Ralang Monastery, the Maenam Hill trek, Kewzing village homestays and Temi tea garden, with Kanchenjunga views on clear mornings.

local_story.title: Rabong, a pass town and a mountain oath
paras: Older maps and many locals still say Rabong or Rabongla. The la at the end is the Bhutia and Tibetan word for a pass, and the town grew on exactly that: a saddle on the shoulder of Maenam Hill, where roads from Namchi, from Gangtok via Singtam and from the Rangeet side at Legship meet. Bhutia, Lepcha and Nepali families farm the slopes around it, and for most of the twentieth century it was a quiet bazaar of tin roofs, tea shops and the Rabong Gompa, with Kanchenjunga filling the north-west horizon on clear winter days.

Ravangla is also where Sikkim's most Sikkimese festival is celebrated with the most energy. Pang Lhabsol, on the fifteenth day of the seventh Tibetan month in August or September, honours Mount Kanchenjunga as the guardian deity of the land. It also remembers the oath of blood brotherhood sworn at Kabi Longtsok by the Lepcha chief Thekong Tek and the Bhutia chief Khye Bumsa, with the mountain as witness. Sikkimese tradition credits the third Chogyal, Chakdor Namgyal, with shaping its warrior dances, which monks still perform in costume.

The town's skyline changed in the 2000s. To mark the 2,550th Buddha Jayanti, the anniversary of the Buddha, the Sikkim government began Tathagata Tsal, now called Buddha Park, beside the Rabong Gompa. Its centrepiece is a Buddha about 130 ft, or 40 m, tall. The 14th Dalai Lama consecrated it in March 2013, and Ravangla went from a jeep stop to a destination. A few kilometres away, Ralang keeps an older layer of the story: an eighteenth-century gompa and a much larger Kagyu monastery built in the 1990s.

did_you_know: The Buddha statue at Tathagata Tsal is about 130 ft (40 m) tall and was consecrated by the 14th Dalai Lama in March 2013.
Pang Lhabsol remembers an oath of brotherhood sworn by the Lepcha chief Thekong Tek and the Bhutia chief Khye Bumsa at Kabi Longtsok, with Kanchenjunga as witness.
Kewzing, a short drive below Ravangla, has a Bon monastery; Bon followers walk around shrines anticlockwise, the opposite direction to Buddhists.
intro: Ravangla is a one-street ridge town with a big view and a slow pace. The main bazaar runs along the road with budget hotels, momo shops and the jeep stand; a short walk away the lawns of Buddha Park lead up to the giant gilded statue. On clear mornings from October to April you see Kanchenjunga and the snow peaks of West Sikkim to the north-west. At about 2,100 m it is cool all year, cold in winter, and wrapped in cloud for much of the monsoon.

Most visitors give it one night on a South Sikkim circuit with Namchi and Temi, but two nights let you do Ralang Monastery, a village walk at Kewzing or Temi tea garden, and the park in the quiet early hours. Ravangla is also a good place to break the journey between Gangtok and Pelling. Food is simple and cheap, rooms are reasonable outside holiday weeks, and shared jeeps link it to Siliguri, Gangtok and Namchi every morning.
facts: Buddha Park, Ralang Monastery, Pang Lhabsol
Jio/Airtel fair in town, weak in villages
costs: Village homestay with dinner and breakfast
Thali or momos in the bazaar

highlights.title: Buddha Park at Tathagata Tsal
highlights.text: Landscaped grounds, prayer wheels and a gilded Buddha about 130 ft tall, with the Rabong Gompa beside it. Come at opening time for quiet lawns and the best chance of a clear Kanchenjunga behind the statue. Allow 1.5–2 hours, and a little longer if you walk the outer path.

highlights.title: Ralang Monastery
highlights.text: About 13 km from town, Ralang has two monasteries: a small eighteenth-century gompa and a large Kagyu monastery built in the 1990s, with painted halls and a big courtyard. Monks gather for prayers in the morning and afternoon, and masked dances are held at certain festivals.

highlights.title: The Maenam Hill trek
highlights.text: A full-day climb from Ravangla through oak, rhododendron and bamboo in the Maenam Wildlife Sanctuary to a summit at about 3,200 m, with wide views over Sikkim on a clear day. It needs a local guide, an early start, a sanctuary fee and good shoes.

highlights.title: Kewzing village
highlights.text: A Bhutia village a short drive below Ravangla with family homestays, cardamom and maize fields, and Yungdrung Kundrakling, one of Sikkim's few Bon monasteries. It is a good place to slow down for a night and eat at a family table rather than a hotel.

highlights.title: Pang Lhabsol in August or September
highlights.text: On the fifteenth day of the seventh Tibetan month, Ravangla holds one of Sikkim's biggest celebrations of Pang Lhabsol, with warrior dances honouring Kanchenjunga as guardian deity. Rooms fill and roads are wet, so book ahead and check the date each year.

highlights.title: Borong hot spring
highlights.text: Below Ralang, on the way down towards the Rangeet, the Borong hot spring draws local families in winter, when bathing is a seasonal tradition. Facilities are simple and access depends on road conditions, so ask in Ravangla before you go and check current status.

how_to_reach.text: Morning shared jeeps run to Ravangla from Siliguri (about ₹300–400 a seat, 4.5–5 hours), from Gangtok (about ₹250–350, 3 hours) and from Namchi (about ₹80–120, 1 hour). In Siliguri ask at the SNT and private Sikkim jeep stands; book your seat the evening before in season. Return jeeps leave Ravangla early, often by 7 or 8 am.

A small car from NJP or Bagdogra costs roughly ₹4,500–5,500 and takes about 4.5–5 hours via Melli and Namchi or via Jorethang. From Gangtok allow about 3 hours via Singtam. From Pelling the drive via Legship takes about 3 hours. Rates rise in holiday weeks; agree the price before you set off.

The nearest railhead is New Jalpaiguri (NJP) and the nearest airport is Bagdogra, both near Siliguri, about 120 km away. Pakyong airport near Gangtok has had irregular flights; check current status before you plan around it. From either gateway you continue by shared jeep or reserved car.

where_to_stay: Most budget hotels and family guesthouses sit along the main road near the Ravangla bazaar and jeep stand, within walking distance of Buddha Park; rooms run about ₹1,200–2,500 a night outside holiday weeks. For more space and gardens, Mt Narsing Village Resort, a long-running cottage resort just outside town, is a comfortable mid-range choice. For a village stay, the homestays of Kewzing, a short drive below Ravangla, give you home cooking and farm walks for about ₹1,500–2,500 per person with meals. Book ahead for Pang Lhabsol and the October holidays.
tips: Visit Buddha Park at opening time, when the lawns are empty and the mountains are most likely to be clear.
Book your morning jeep seat out of Ravangla the evening before, as most departures leave by 8 am.
Carry a warm layer even in May, since evenings at 2,100 m turn cold quickly once the cloud rolls in.
Walk clockwise around Buddhist stupas and prayer wheels, but follow the anticlockwise custom at the Bon monastery in Kewzing.
Combine Ravangla with Temi and Namchi on one circuit, using shared jeeps between them to keep costs low.

experiences.title: Buddha Park in the quiet first hour
experiences.summary: Walk into Tathagata Tsal as the gates open, circle the 130 ft gilded Buddha with the prayer wheels, look into the hall at its base and, on a clear morning, see Kanchenjunga behind it. Then visit the old Rabong Gompa next door before the tour cars arrive.
body: Buddha Park, officially Tathagata Tsal, was built by the Sikkim government to mark the 2,550th Buddha Jayanti and consecrated by the 14th Dalai Lama in March 2013. From the gate a long, straight path climbs gently between lawns and flower beds towards the statue, which sits on a raised base above the ridge. The Buddha is about 130 ft tall and covered in gold-coloured finish, with the hand held in the earth-touching gesture. On a clear day the Kanchenjunga range stands to the north-west.

Go at opening time. In the first hour the park is quiet, the light is soft and the mountains are most likely to be out; by late morning in holiday weeks it fills with tour groups and cloud often rises from the valleys. Walk the circuit around the statue clockwise, turning the prayer wheels as local visitors do. The base of the statue holds a hall with paintings and displays on the life of the Buddha; photography rules inside change, so follow the signs.

Leave time for the Rabong Gompa beside the park, a working monastery that predates the statue by decades and feels far more lived in. Morning prayers, the sound of horns and the smell of butter lamps are the counterweight to the scale of the new park. Entry to the park is a small fee, roughly ₹50–100 for Indians and more for foreign nationals; hours and fees change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What are Buddha Park Ravangla's timings and entry fee?
faqs.a: The park usually opens in the morning and closes in the late afternoon, around 5 pm, with a small entry fee of roughly ₹50–100 for Indian visitors and a higher fee for foreign nationals. Timings and fees change and may differ on festival days, so check at the gate or with your hotel the day before.

faqs.q: How tall is the Buddha statue at Ravangla?
faqs.a: The Buddha at Tathagata Tsal, Ravangla, is about 130 ft, or roughly 40 m, tall. It was built to mark the 2,550th Buddha Jayanti and consecrated by the 14th Dalai Lama in March 2013. It stands on a raised base on the ridge, so it is visible from many points around the town.

faqs.q: Can you see Kanchenjunga from Buddha Park?
faqs.a: On clear mornings, yes. The Kanchenjunga range rises to the north-west of the park, and photographers like to frame it with the statue. The best chances are October to December and early spring, in the first hours after opening. From June to September and on most afternoons, cloud usually hides the mountains.

experiences.title: Ralang, the old gompa and the new monastery
experiences.cost: Free · donation welcome; car about ₹1,200–1,800 return
experiences.summary: A short drive from Ravangla, Ralang has two monasteries a little apart: an eighteenth-century gompa and the large Kagyu Ralang Palchen Choeling from the 1990s. Go in the morning for prayers, painted halls and a courtyard that comes alive with masked dances at festival time.
body: Ralang lies about 13 km from Ravangla, a 30–40 minute drive down a winding road through farmland and forest. The big monastery, Ralang Palchen Choeling, belongs to the Kagyu school of Tibetan Buddhism and was built in the 1990s. Its main hall is large and richly painted, with tall images and rows of seats for the monks, and a wide courtyard in front. Many young monks study here, so mornings and late afternoons bring prayer sessions with horns, drums and chanting.

The older Ralang gompa, a little distance from the new monastery, dates from the eighteenth century and is much smaller and quieter. The contrast is the point of the visit: one building shows how monasteries in Sikkim looked for centuries, the other how Tibetan Buddhist communities rebuilt and expanded after the 1950s. Ask a monk or your driver which building is open, and remove shoes, cover shoulders and ask before taking photos inside any prayer hall.

Ralang is known for masked cham dances at certain festivals, including around Pang Lhabsol and in the winter months; exact dates follow the Tibetan calendar and change each year, so check current status before you travel. On ordinary days the visit takes one to two hours. A reserved car from Ravangla for the return trip costs roughly ₹1,200–1,800; you can combine it with the Borong side or with Kewzing on the way back.

faqs.q: How far is Ralang Monastery from Ravangla?
faqs.a: About 13 km, roughly 30–40 minutes by car on a narrow hill road. There is no reliable shared jeep for this short hop, so most visitors take a reserved car, which costs roughly ₹1,200–1,800 for the return trip with waiting time. Some fit walkers walk one way downhill and take a car back up.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee at Ralang Monastery?
faqs.a: There is usually no fixed entry fee at Ralang's monasteries, and a small donation in the box is welcome. Dress modestly, remove shoes before entering prayer halls and ask before taking photographs inside. Hours depend on prayer and teaching schedules, so mornings are the most reliable time to find halls open.

faqs.q: When are the masked dances at Ralang?
faqs.a: Ralang holds cham, or masked dances, at certain festivals, including around Pang Lhabsol in August or September and in the winter months. Dates follow the Tibetan lunar calendar and change each year, so check with the monastery, Sikkim Tourism or your Ravangla hotel before planning a trip around them, and book rooms early for festival days.

experiences.title: Day trek to Maenam Hill above Ravangla
experiences.summary: A long, steady climb from Ravangla through the forests of Maenam Wildlife Sanctuary to a summit at about 3,200 m, with views across Sikkim when the sky is clear. Not technical, but a full day that needs a local guide, fitness and an early start.
body: Maenam Hill rises behind Ravangla to about 3,200 m, and its slopes form the Maenam Wildlife Sanctuary. The trail leaves from near the town and climbs through temperate forest of oak, magnolia, rhododendron and dense bamboo, the habitat of red panda, barking deer and many birds, though wildlife is rarely seen on a busy trail. The path is steady rather than technical, but it is long: plan on 4–5 hours up and about 3–4 hours down, with breaks.

Near the top a rock outcrop called Bhaledunga juts from the ridge; the Nepali name is usually explained as rooster rock, after its shape. On a clear morning the summit gives views over large parts of Sikkim, with Kanchenjunga and its neighbours to the north-west and the Rangeet and Teesta valleys falling away below. In spring parts of the trail flower with rhododendrons. In monsoon the path is slippery and full of leeches, and views are rare.

Hire a local guide in Ravangla, about ₹1,500–2,500 for the day, and ask your hotel to arrange it the evening before. The trail passes through a sanctuary, so an entry fee or permit from the forest office may apply; rules change, so check current status before you travel. Start by 6 am, carry 2 litres of water, a packed lunch, a rain jacket and a warm layer, and turn back by early afternoon wherever you are.

faqs.q: How difficult is the Maenam Hill trek?
faqs.a: Moderate to demanding because of its length rather than any technical section. You climb roughly 1,100 m from Ravangla to about 3,200 m and back in one day, usually 8–9 hours with breaks. Regular walkers manage it; first-time trekkers should be fit and start very early. Children and older travellers are better off with shorter forest walks near town.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide or permit for Maenam Hill?
faqs.a: A local guide is strongly advised because forest trails branch and cloud can roll in quickly; expect about ₹1,500–2,500 for the day. The route lies in Maenam Wildlife Sanctuary, so an entry fee or forest permit may be required. Ask your hotel or the forest office in Ravangla the day before, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the best season for the Maenam trek?
faqs.a: October to December gives the clearest views and dry trails. March to May brings rhododendron flowers and warmer days, with more afternoon haze. Avoid June to September, when the trail is slippery, leeches are common and the summit is usually in cloud. In January and February, frost and occasional snow can make the upper trail icy.

experiences.title: Kewzing village homestay and Bon monastery
experiences.summary: Spend a night with a Bhutia farming family in Kewzing, a short drive below Ravangla, walk through cardamom and maize fields, and visit Yungdrung Kundrakling, one of Sikkim's few monasteries of the Bon faith. A slower, warmer side of South Sikkim than the big statue on the ridge.
body: Kewzing is a village of Bhutia families on the slopes below Ravangla, on the road that heads down towards Legship and the Rangeet valley. Several households run homestays with simple rooms, home-cooked food and a lot of local knowledge. Days here follow the farm: maize, vegetables, large cardamom in the shaded gullies, cows and a kitchen garden. Hosts often take guests on short walks to viewpoints, a village chorten or a nearby stream.

Kewzing is also home to Yungdrung Kundrakling, a monastery of the Bon faith. Bon is the old religious tradition of Tibet, which shares much with Tibetan Buddhism but keeps its own lineages and customs. Bon followers walk around shrines and turn prayer wheels anticlockwise, the reverse of Buddhist practice, so watch what local visitors do and follow them. Ask before photographing inside, keep voices low, and leave a small donation.

Dinner in a Kewzing homestay is usually rice, dal, a green such as nettle or mustard leaves, potatoes or squash, pickles and often pork, chicken or churpi dishes; breakfast may be roti, sel roti or Tibetan-style bread with tea. Expect to pay about ₹1,500–2,500 per person with dinner and breakfast, indicative, in cash. A reserved car from Ravangla takes 15–25 minutes; agree the fare first, or ask your host to arrange the pickup.

faqs.q: How far is Kewzing from Ravangla?
faqs.a: Kewzing is a short drive below Ravangla on the road towards Legship, usually 15–25 minutes by car depending on which part of the village your homestay is in. Shared jeeps heading for Legship pass through, but timings are irregular, so most visitors take a local taxi from Ravangla or ask their homestay host to arrange a pickup.

faqs.q: What is the Bon monastery in Kewzing?
faqs.a: Yungdrung Kundrakling in Kewzing is a monastery of the Bon faith, the old religious tradition of Tibet that runs alongside Tibetan Buddhism with its own lineages, texts and customs. It is one of very few Bon monasteries in Sikkim. Visitors are welcome at reasonable hours; walk around shrines anticlockwise, as Bon followers do, and ask before taking photos.

faqs.q: Are Kewzing homestays good for families?
faqs.a: Yes. Kewzing homestays are run by families, rooms are simple and clean, food is home cooked and mild on request, and there is space for children to walk around the fields. Expect basic bathrooms and hot water that may come by bucket. Rates run about ₹1,500–2,500 per person with dinner and breakfast; confirm what is included when you book.

faqs.q: Is Ravangla worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, for one or two nights on a South Sikkim circuit. Ravangla has the 130 ft Buddha at Buddha Park, the old and new monasteries of Ralang, village homestays at Kewzing, the Maenam Hill trek and Kanchenjunga views on clear mornings. It is quieter and cooler than Namchi and a good base for Temi tea garden.

faqs.q: How do I reach Ravangla from Siliguri or NJP?
faqs.a: Take a morning shared jeep from Siliguri to Ravangla, about ₹300–400 a seat and 4.5–5 hours, or a jeep to Namchi or Jorethang and change. A reserved small car from NJP or Bagdogra costs roughly ₹4,500–5,500. The distance is about 120 km. Book jeep seats a day ahead in holiday weeks and check road status in the monsoon.

faqs.q: How far is Ravangla from Gangtok?
faqs.a: About 65 km, roughly 3 hours by road via Singtam. Shared jeeps run in the morning from Gangtok for about ₹250–350 a seat; a reserved car costs more and lets you stop at Temi tea garden on the way. Roads can be slow after heavy rain, so start early in the monsoon months.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Ravangla?
faqs.a: March to May and October to December. Spring brings flowers and mild days, and autumn the clearest Kanchenjunga views. January and February are cold, sometimes with frost, but often clear. June to September is the monsoon, with cloud, rain and occasional landslides, though Pang Lhabsol in August or September draws visitors who do not mind the weather.

faqs.q: How many days are enough for Ravangla?
faqs.a: One night covers Buddha Park and a look around town. Two nights let you add Ralang Monastery, a walk or overnight at Kewzing, or a day trip to Temi tea garden. Add a third day if you want to trek to Maenam Hill, which takes a full day with an early start and a local guide.

faqs.q: Do Indians or foreigners need a permit for Ravangla?
faqs.a: Indian citizens do not need a permit for Ravangla or the rest of South Sikkim. Foreign nationals need a Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, available online as an e-RAP or at entry points such as Rangpo and Melli, before entering Sikkim. Trekking in sanctuaries such as Maenam may need a forest entry fee. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the weather like in Ravangla?
faqs.a: Cool all year because of the altitude of about 2,100 m. Summer days are mild, around 15–20 °C, with cool nights. Winter days are crisp and nights drop near freezing from December to February. The monsoon from June to September brings heavy rain and thick cloud. Pack a warm jacket in every season except perhaps May.

faqs.q: Where can I eat in Ravangla?
faqs.a: The bazaar along the main road has small restaurants and momo shops serving thali, momos, thukpa, chowmein and tea, with a meal costing about ₹80–250. Hotels serve simple Indian and Chinese dishes. For local food such as nettle soup, churpi and pork with greens, stay in a homestay at Kewzing or ask your hotel kitchen in advance.

faqs.q: When is Pang Lhabsol at Ravangla?
faqs.a: Pang Lhabsol falls on the fifteenth day of the seventh month of the Tibetan calendar, which lands in August or September. Ravangla hosts one of Sikkim's biggest celebrations, with warrior dances honouring Kanchenjunga as guardian deity. The date changes every year, so check the current calendar with Sikkim Tourism and book a room well ahead.
